prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the mortgage-underwriting agent (residential mortgage applications and remortgages) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: illness affecting income. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When illness has reduced income, I should separate a short absence from a longer-term change and ask whether the customer expects a return to full earnings, because the affordability approach differs materially between the two."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the applicant is in receipt of sick pay, I should confirm whether it is occupational or statutory and how long it lasts, because the remaining duration can affect what income is sustainable for underwriting."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the customer has variable earnings, I should check whether illness has only affected recent months and whether I can reasonably use a longer average, rather than over-weighting a temporary dip."},{"type":"preference","content":"When evidence is available, I prefer to see employer confirmation, benefits letters, or clinician correspondence that explains the likely timescale of recovery, because it helps me distinguish temporary disruption from ongoing affordability risk."},{"type":"observation","content":"When illness is linked to a condition likely to recur, I should be cautious about assuming the latest income is fully restored, even if the customer has returned to work, because recurrence can undermine the budget after completion."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a household relies on one main income and that earner has been ill, I should test the case more carefully for resilience, because there may be limited buffer if earnings fall again."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the applicant has recently moved from full pay to reduced pay, I should look for stable post-illness earnings over time before I treat the reduced figure as the new norm, unless the evidence clearly supports it."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the customer is clear and consistent about treatment, recovery, and work plans, I prefer to keep the review focused on affordability rather than searching for unnecessary medical detail, because the key issue is income sustainability."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a remortgage is being considered, I should pay attention to whether the current lender’s payment history has remained strong through the illness, because that can be a useful indicator of practical affordability."},{"type":"fact","content":"When illness has caused exceptional one-off costs as well as lower income, I should not count on those costs disappearing immediately, because ongoing care, travel, or medication can continue to suppress disposable income."}]}
